meta.title: How a Russia-NATO War Would Actually Unfold
meta.working_title: How a Russia-NATO War Would Actually Unfold (a War-Game Scenario)
meta.device: A big NATO war-room table map of Europe. A 'race clock' in the corner counts the days NATO needs to reach the front against the hours Russia needs to grab the Baltics. Blue NATO arrows crawl east; red arrows push west. Every obstacle (a port hack, a burning signal box, the 8.5 cm rail gap) drops a red 'DELAY' tag on the clock.
meta.style: Map-driven war-game explainer in the house 2D style, Alium character style (as in BlackRock). Painted plates: a NATO headquarters war room, a foggy Baltic border with dragon's-teeth concrete blocks, a Texas cargo port at dawn, a stormy North Atlantic, a German rail yard at night, a narrow Polish-Lithuanian farm corridor, a Gotland harbour. Steel blue, olive and warning red. All soldiers generic with no real insignia. Putin and the US president never shown, named only in narration. SFX under the VO (radar pings, ship horns, jet roar, drone buzz, train clatter), music only at combine.
meta.source: English transcript 'How Would a War With Russia Unfold?' (~2,900 words), fully rewritten in our own words. Sponsor read and interview clips cut; the guest's points paraphrased. Framed throughout as a fictional scenario built from war games and NATO assessments.

shots.vo: Before dawn, Russian tanks cross into Estonia and Latvia. Swarms of drones fly ahead of them. A second force pushes into Lithuania from Belarus.
shots.visual: The war-room map: red arrows cross the Baltic borders; drone dots buzz ahead.
shots.anim: Red arrows push in; drone dots swarm.

shots.vo: Within hours, NATO invokes Article 5. An attack on one member is an attack on all of them. Now the whole alliance is at war.
shots.visual: A council table; 32 flags light up one after another.
shots.anim: Flags light up in a chain.

shots.vo: This is a made-up scenario, built from real war games and NATO assessments. But it shows the race that would decide everything: how fast can NATO get to the front?
shots.visual: A race clock: Russia's hours against NATO's days.
shots.anim: Two clocks tick; one runs much faster.

shots.visual: Title over the war-room map.
shots.onscreen: HOW A RUSSIA-NATO WAR WOULD UNFOLD
shots.anim: Map pulses; title slams in.

acts.name: Act 1: Grab It Before Anyone Arrives

shots.vo: In Belgium sits SHAPE, NATO's military headquarters. Its commander, the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, gets the call: Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius are under attack.
shots.visual: A war room with a giant table map; officers turning to the phone.
shots.anim: Phone rings; officers crowd the map.

shots.vo: Russia's likely plan is called a fait accompli. Grab the land fast, dig in, and dare NATO to start a much bigger war to take it back.
shots.visual: A red flag planted on the Baltic map; a fence goes up around it.
shots.anim: Flag stabs in; fence pops up.

shots.vo: In a famous war game by the RAND think tank, Russian forces reached the Baltic capitals in about 36 to 60 hours.
shots.visual: A stopwatch over the map; three capital pins turn red.
shots.anim: Stopwatch spins; pins flip red.

shots.vo: The three Baltic states are small. Together they have about six million people, and they border Russia or its ally Belarus on almost every land side.
shots.visual: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania on the map, squeezed between Russia, Belarus and the sea.
shots.anim: Neighbours lean in; Baltics sweat.

shots.vo: So every hour they hold out matters. Each day of delay gives NATO time to arrive.
shots.visual: The race clock; each hour held adds a blue tick.
shots.anim: Ticks fill in blue.

shots.vo: That is why the Baltic borders are being turned into obstacle courses. Rows of concrete 'dragon's teeth' are built to stop tanks.
shots.visual: A foggy border; rows of concrete pyramids across a field.
shots.anim: Fog drifts; a tank stops at the teeth.

shots.vo: In 2025 all three countries said they would leave the treaty that bans anti-personnel landmines. In this scenario, the borders are mined.
shots.visual: A treaty page torn; warning signs with a skull spring up along the border.
shots.anim: Treaty rips; signs pop up in a row.

shots.vo: Lithuania is wiring its border with cameras and sound sensors, so it knows the moment anything crosses.
shots.visual: Sensor posts along a treeline, each blinking as a shape passes.
shots.anim: Sensors blink in a wave.

shots.vo: It is even bringing back old swamps and forests, to push enemy columns into a few narrow roads.
shots.visual: A dry field flooding into marsh; trees sprouting; a tank column squeezed onto one road.
shots.anim: Water spreads; trees pop up; tanks bunch.

shots.vo: And here NATO had warning. Like Ukraine in 2022, the alliance saw troops massing and started moving before the first shot.
shots.visual: Satellite photos of tank rows pinned to a board; NATO officers pointing.
shots.anim: Photos slide in; red circles appear.

shots.vo: But warning only helps if you can move. And moving an army across Europe is much harder than it sounds.
shots.visual: A blue arrow on the map tries to move east and stalls.
shots.anim: Arrow lurches, stops, spins its wheels.

shots.vo: On paper NATO is huge: about 3.4 million active troops, more than twice Russia's. Most of them are American, Turkish or French.
shots.visual: Two stacks of soldier icons, NATO's much taller.
shots.anim: Stacks grow; NATO's towers over.

shots.vo: For a war like this, NATO's commander might need to move hundreds of thousands of them to the eastern flank.
shots.visual: Blue arrows from all over Europe pointing east.
shots.anim: Arrows sprout from every base.

shots.vo: Right now, moving troops from Europe's Atlantic coast to its eastern edge could take up to 45 days. NATO wants that under 10.
shots.visual: A calendar flipping to day 45; a target sticker says 10.
shots.anim: Pages flip; a red sticker slaps on.

shots.vo: About 80,000 to 100,000 American troops are already in Europe. More would come from the United States: tanks from Texas, soldiers from Georgia.
shots.visual: A US map with two pins; dotted lines arc across the Atlantic.
shots.anim: Pins pop; lines arc over the ocean.

shots.vo: At the port of Beaumont in Texas, vehicles roll into a giant cargo ship built to carry an army's gear.
shots.visual: A dawn port; tanks and trucks roll up a ramp into a huge ship.
shots.anim: Vehicles roll aboard; cranes swing.

shots.vo: It heads out through the Gulf of Mexico and across the Atlantic. The crossing takes about two weeks.
shots.visual: The ship sails out past the coast; a dotted route across the ocean map.
shots.anim: Ship pulls away; route draws itself.

shots.vo: Russia has one of the world's biggest submarine fleets. Many patrol the North Atlantic, near the gap between Greenland, Iceland and Britain.
shots.visual: A stormy ocean; dark submarine shapes under the waves.
shots.anim: Waves crash; sonar pings ring out.

shots.vo: Some subs can cut undersea data cables. Others hunt ships. And sea mines can close a whole shipping lane.
shots.visual: Cross-section: a cable on the seabed, a mine bobbing on its chain.
shots.anim: Cable sparks; mine sways.

shots.vo: Our ship makes it to the North Sea, nearly at Rotterdam. Then the port's computer systems go dark. A cyber attack.
shots.visual: Port control room screens flicker to red error messages.
shots.anim: Screens glitch and go red.

shots.vo: The captain can't wait. He turns for Bremerhaven in Germany instead. US forces have practised using ports all over Europe for exactly this reason.
shots.visual: The map: the ship's route bends from Rotterdam to Bremerhaven.
shots.anim: Route snaps to a new port; DELAY tag drops.

shots.vo: Meanwhile soldiers from Fort Stewart, Georgia, board ordinary airliners. The US military can borrow commercial jets in a crisis.
shots.visual: Soldiers with kit bags walking up the steps of a passenger jet.
shots.anim: Line of soldiers boards; jet taxis.

shots.vo: Over the Baltics, the fight for the sky has already started. Russia sends its most advanced fighters, Su-57s.
shots.visual: Two dark jets streak across a cold sky.
shots.anim: Jets roar past with contrails.

shots.vo: At a German airbase, two Eurofighter Typhoons scramble. They can be in the air within 15 minutes and reach the eastern flank in about an hour.
shots.visual: Pilots sprinting to jets; canopies close; jets take off.
shots.anim: Pilots run; jets lift off.

shots.vo: But much of the war happens lower down, with drones. They are cheap, and the missiles used to shoot them down often cost far more.
shots.visual: A cheap drone next to a price tag; an expensive missile with a bigger price tag.
shots.anim: Price tags pop; bigger one wobbles.

shots.vo: Russia builds drones on a huge scale. Recon drones like the Orlan-10 spot targets for hours, then guide in the attack drones.
shots.visual: A small recon drone circling; its camera view marks a target.
shots.anim: Drone circles; red box locks on.

shots.vo: The Geran-2, Russia's copy of Iran's Shahed drone, can fly more than 1,000 kilometres and crash into its target with a large warhead.
shots.visual: A triangle-winged drone flying low over a map toward a dot.
shots.anim: Drone buzzes along the route.

shots.vo: The Baltics are arming themselves with drones too. One Lithuanian officer has said cheap drones could do most of the damage to an invading force.
shots.visual: Baltic soldiers holding small quadcopters; a swarm lifts off.
shots.anim: Swarm lifts; screens flicker.

shots.vo: Back on the ground, the tanks unload at Bremerhaven. Now they must cross Germany by train.
shots.visual: A night rail yard; tanks being chained onto flatcars.
shots.anim: Chains clank; train starts rolling.

shots.vo: The route east runs along the North Sea-Baltic corridor, one of Europe's main transport arteries. But much of Germany's rail network is old and overloaded.
shots.visual: The corridor glowing across the map; old signal boxes and rusty bridges along it.
shots.anim: Route lights up; a bridge creaks.

shots.vo: Then comes a tiny problem: 8.5 centimetres. Baltic railways still use the wider Soviet-era gauge, so trains can't simply roll straight through.
shots.visual: Two rail tracks side by side; a ruler shows the gap.
shots.anim: Ruler slides in; wheels miss the rail.

shots.vo: A new standard-gauge line, Rail Baltica, should fix that. It was due in 2026. The target is now 2030, and some fear even later.
shots.visual: A half-built railway ending in a field; a calendar flipping years.
shots.anim: Calendar flips; track ends in mud.

shots.vo: And in our scenario, saboteurs strike. Shadowy figures set fire to a railway signal box. The military train has to stop until the signals work again.
shots.visual: Night: a signal box on fire; a train halted with red lights.
shots.anim: Flames flicker; train brakes squeal; DELAY tag.

shots.vo: Some countries fence off their railways. Germany relies mostly on cameras and drones, and its rail operator says the network is simply too big to guard everywhere.
shots.visual: An endless track stretching into the dark, one lonely camera post.
shots.anim: Camera turns; track vanishes into fog.

shots.vo: Then every NATO convoy hits the same bottleneck: the Suwałki Gap, a strip of land along the Polish-Lithuanian border.
shots.visual: A narrow farm corridor between two dark regions on the map.
shots.anim: Map zooms into a narrow strip.

shots.vo: It is only about 65 kilometres wide. On one side is Kaliningrad, a heavily armed piece of Russia. On the other is Belarus, Russia's closest ally.
shots.visual: Kaliningrad and Belarus on either side, guns pointing at the gap.
shots.anim: Both sides glare; gap narrows.

shots.vo: Missiles, drones and artillery from both sides could turn the roads into a gauntlet. If the gap closes, the Baltics can only be reached by sea or air.
shots.visual: Convoys on the road under falling shells; the gap snaps shut.
shots.anim: Explosions bloom; gate slams.

shots.vo: That makes the Baltic Sea vital, and one island most of all: Gotland, owned by Sweden, a NATO member since 2024.
shots.visual: A rocky island harbour in the middle of the Baltic Sea.
shots.anim: Waves; a flag snaps in the wind.

shots.vo: Experts call it an unsinkable aircraft carrier. Jets from Gotland could hit Russian supply lines, and Sweden says it could be ready for action within days.
shots.visual: The island on the map with jet icons launching from it.
shots.anim: Jets launch; range circles spread.

shots.vo: How the war goes from here is impossible to predict. This scenario is fiction. But Russia's pressure on Europe is not.
shots.visual: The war-room map fades to real headlines: sabotage, cyber attacks, drones over airports.
shots.anim: Headlines slide in one by one.

shots.vo: For years Europe has faced sabotage, assassination plots, cyber attacks and mystery drones. Since 2022, defence spending has jumped, especially in Germany.
shots.visual: A bar chart of European defence spending climbing.
shots.anim: Bars rise year by year.

shots.vo: Our scenario assumed America shows up in full. That is not guaranteed. The US president has openly questioned how far America would go to defend some allies.
shots.visual: A blue NATO arrow from the US flickers and turns dashed.
shots.anim: Arrow flickers between solid and dashed.

shots.vo: Meanwhile Ukraine has held Russia's army back for years. In doing so, it is buying the rest of Europe something it badly needs: time.
shots.visual: The race clock again; Ukraine on the map holding a shield; the clock slows.
shots.anim: Clock hands slow; shield glows.

shots.visual: End card.
shots.onscreen: HOW A RUSSIA-NATO WAR WOULD UNFOLD
shots.anim: Title holds; map glows.

hooks: Day one. Russian tanks cross into Estonia before dawn. NATO has hours to stop them and weeks to get there.
If Russia attacked NATO tomorrow, the war would be decided by a 65-kilometre strip of farmland.

fixes: Framed as a fictional scenario from war games and assessments, as the source did; nothing presented as a prediction.
RAND 2016 war games: Russian forces reached Tallinn/Riga in 36 to 60 hours (added; source had no figure).
Baltic states' combined population about 6 million (added).
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania (with Poland and Finland) announced withdrawal from the Ottawa landmine treaty in 2025.
NATO active personnel about 3.4 million vs Russia about 1.3 million (source said 3.6M and 'almost three times'); kept as 'more than twice'.
Source's '800,000 soldiers' figure dropped as unsourced; script says 'hundreds of thousands'.
US troops in Europe roughly 80,000-100,000 (source said 86,000); stated as a range.
Atlantic sealift crossing about 10-14 days (added as 'about two weeks').
Source's '64 active submarines' and '400 drones a day' dropped as unverified; kept as 'one of the biggest fleets' and 'huge scale'.
Geran-2: Russian-built Shahed-136, range over 1,000 km; warhead size kept general ('large warhead').
Eurofighter QRA readiness 15 minutes; top speed and altitude figures cut.
Rail gauge: 1,520 mm vs 1,435 mm = 85 mm (8.5 cm). Rail Baltica completion now targeted around 2030.
Suwałki Gap about 65 km between Kaliningrad and Belarus. Sweden joined NATO March 2024.
Guest interview quotes (retired US Army Europe commander) paraphrased, not quoted. US president's clip cut; no leaders shown on screen.
cuts: Interview clips cut; the guest's points paraphrased.
US president's quote clip removed; one neutral line kept.
German budget figure for Ukraine aid dropped as unclear.
Everything rewritten in our own words.
